hook: The Legend of Zelda's whole musical structure is a direct descendant of a 19th-century opera technique.
script: The Legend of Zelda's whole musical structure is a direct descendant of a 19th-century opera technique. Composer Koji Kondo builds specific musical themes for characters, places, and items across the series, so you learn to recognize what's happening before you even see it — a fairy fountain sting, a puzzle-solved jingle, Zelda's own theme. That's a leitmotif, and the technique traces straight back to Wagner's Ring Cycle, where he used the exact same idea across four operas in the 1800s. Kondo didn't invent this. He inherited it, and then built one of gaming's most recognizable musical languages on top of it. Nintendo and 19th-century German opera are running on the same trick.

hook: I work in tech, so I get asked constantly whether AI can just write classical music now. The honest answer is more interesting than yes or no.
script: I work in tech, so I get asked constantly whether AI can just write classical music now. The honest answer is more interesting than a yes or no. Tools like AIVA, Google's Magenta project, and Suno can generate technically coherent music fast, and for background or functional music, that's genuinely useful. What they're still bad at is the thing that actually makes a piece of classical music work — long-range structure, a musical idea that develops and pays off forty minutes later, the kind of large-scale architecture a symphony needs. AI is good at generating something that sounds plausible for thirty seconds. It's not yet good at building something that earns an ending. That gap is exactly where composers are still doing work no tool can replace.

hook: Marian Anderson didn't debut at the Met until 1955 — and only after being banned from a concert hall sixteen years earlier for being Black.
script: Marian Anderson didn't debut at the Metropolitan Opera until January 7th, 1955 — the first Black singer to perform there, singing Ulrica in Verdi's Un ballo in maschera. The audience gave her a standing ovation before she'd even sung a note. That moment only happened because of a specific person: Rudolf Bing, who took over as the Met's general manager in 1950 and deliberately worked to integrate its casting. But get the fuller timeline: in 1939, sixteen years earlier, the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let Anderson sing to an integrated audience at Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C. She performed for 75,000 people on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial instead. Her Met debut opened the door for Leontyne Price, Grace Bumbry, and Jessye Norman after her. Sixteen years between the ban and the ovation is the part of this story that deserves to be said out loud, not just implied.
caption: Marian Anderson debuted at the Met in 1955 — 16 years after being banned from a concert hall

hook: Leontyne Price became so identified with one specific opera role that critics of her era just called her 'the Aida.'
script: Leontyne Price became so identified with one specific opera role that critics of her era just called her 'the Aida.' She made her Met debut in 1961 alongside Franco Corelli, but Verdi's Aida became her signature — Herbert von Karajan personally conducted her in the role for her European debut at the Vienna State Opera in 1958, and she recorded two separate Grammy-winning versions of the opera for RCA. Her farewell performance as Aida at the Met in 1985 was filmed for PBS broadcast, closing out a career that helped open the door for Black singers at major American opera houses for decades after her. One role, one voice, decades of being considered simply definitive at it.

Nkeiru Okoye, a Guggenheim Fellow, has written a full opera on Harriet Tubman and, more recently, 'When the Caged Bird Sings,' which premiered at the University of Michigan in February 2024 — a piece that blends oratorio, theater, and opera into what Okoye herself calls 'a gathering,' partly in tribute to Maya Angelou. Her work sits deliberately at the intersection of classical tradition and African American musical history, and it's exactly the kind of composer this space should be naming constantly and mostly isn't.

hook: One of classical music's most in-demand living composers started on the violin in a Lower East Side settlement school.
script: One of classical music's most in-demand living composers started on the violin in a Lower East Side settlement school. Jessie Montgomery trained at Juilliard, became the Chicago Symphony Orchestra's composer-in-residence in 2021, and was named one of three composers of color in the Metropolitan Opera's commissioning program — meaning the Met is actively paying her to write new work for its stage, not just occasionally programming something she already wrote. Her music pulls in samba, Zimbabwean dance rhythms, swing, and techno alongside classical structure, and she's cited Florence Price as a direct influence, the same way earlier composers cited Brahms or Beethoven. This is what it actually looks like when an institution puts real money behind expanding who gets to write its future repertoire, not just its past.

hook: A composer who builds classical works around Peruvian folk instruments just won the Pulitzer Prize for Music.
script: A composer who builds classical works around Peruvian folk instruments just won the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Gabriela Lena Frank, whose mother is Peruvian and father is of Lithuanian Jewish heritage, writes for Western classical ensembles while pulling in the sounds of Andean instruments like the pan flute and the charango — one 2012 piece was written to be performed entirely on indigenous instruments. She'd already received a Heinz Award in 2020 specifically recognizing how she 'breaks gender, disability, and cultural barriers in classical music composition,' and the Pulitzer this year is the field's biggest possible confirmation that this approach isn't a niche side lane. It's just composition.

hook: In 2021, a Cuban-American composer named Tania León won the Pulitzer Prize for Music for a piece called 'Stride' — and her resume is wild.
script: In 2021, Cuban-American composer Tania León won the Pulitzer Prize for Music for her piece 'Stride.' She's spent decades working as both a composer and a conductor, and she co-founded the music program at the Dance Theatre of Harlem earlier in her career — that kind of range doesn't happen by accident. Her win also made her the first Black woman to receive the award in its history, which is worth naming precisely rather than rounding up into a bigger headline than it is. Have you listened to 'Stride' yet? It's worth pulling up before you keep scrolling.
